title: Visitor Pattern
summary: Adding a new operation across an entire object hierarchy without modifying the hierarchy itself, at the cost of the classes knowing about the visitor.

slides.markdown:
**Visitor** lets you add a whole new operation across a family of classes — an AST, a document tree, a shape hierarchy — without touching any of those classes again. A compiler adding a new pass (type-checking, code generation) over the same AST node types doesn't edit every node class; it writes one new `Visitor` implementation instead.

The trade-off is real: it works cleanly only when the *hierarchy* is stable and the *operations* over it are what keep growing — flip that assumption and Visitor becomes the wrong tool, as later pitfalls cover.

slides.sectionTitle: The problem Visitor solves: adding a new operation across an object hierarchy without touching each class
slides.markdown:
An AST has node classes `NumberNode`, `BinaryOpNode`, `VariableNode`. You need to add a `print()` operation, then later a `typeCheck()` operation, then later a `codeGen()` operation — each one needs different logic for every node type.

The naive approach adds a method to every node class per operation: `NumberNode.print()`, `NumberNode.typeCheck()`, `NumberNode.codeGen()`, repeated for every node class. Every new operation means editing every existing class, and those classes accumulate more and more unrelated responsibilities that have nothing to do with what a `NumberNode` fundamentally is.

The underlying problem: new operations arrive over time, and each one cuts across every class in the hierarchy — but adding methods to every class means the classes themselves must be reopened and re-tested for every unrelated new operation.

slides.sectionTitle: Double dispatch: how accept/visit picks the right method for both the element and the operation
slides.markdown:
Each node class gets exactly one new method, `accept(visitor)`, that simply calls `visitor.visitNumberNode(this)` (or the matching method for its own type). A `Visitor` interface declares one `visitX()` method per node type — `visitNumberNode()`, `visitBinaryOpNode()`, `visitVariableNode()`.

This two-step call is **double dispatch**: `node.accept(visitor)` first resolves which node's `accept()` runs (based on the node's actual type), and that `accept()` then calls the matching `visitX()` on the visitor (based on the node's type again, but named explicitly this time) — landing on the exact right combination of node-type and operation without a single `if (node instanceof ...)` check anywhere.

Adding a new operation means writing one new `Visitor` implementation with all its `visitX()` methods — no node class is touched.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a visitor traversing a hierarchy, method resolution shown at each node
slides.markdown:
Traversing a tree with a visitor means calling `accept(visitor)` on the root, which recurses into children, each calling its own `accept(visitor)` — and each node's `accept()` dispatches to the visitor's type-matched method.

![A BinaryOpNode root with NumberNode and VariableNode children, each dispatching accept(visitor) to a Visitor's type-matched visit methods](assets/visitor-ast.svg)

The same tree can be handed to a `PrintVisitor`, then a `TypeCheckVisitor`, then a `CodeGenVisitor` — the tree's structure and traversal logic never change; only which visitor object walks it does.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: implementing a Visitor over an AST
Compare: Visitor vs adding a method to every class — when the pattern earns its complexity
slides.markdown:
| | Visitor | Method on every class |
|---|---|---|
| Adding a new operation | One new Visitor class, no node classes touched | Add a method to every existing node class |
| Adding a new node/element type | Every existing Visitor implementation needs a new visitX() method | One new class with the needed methods; nothing else changes |
| Where logic lives | Grouped by operation (all of PrintVisitor's logic together) | Scattered by class (each node's print logic lives in that node) |
| Best fit | Stable hierarchy, frequently added operations | Stable set of operations, frequently added element types |

**How to decide:** ask which axis actually changes more often for this codebase — new node/element types, or new operations over existing ones — and pick the pattern that keeps the *frequent* change cheap, even if it makes the rare change more expensive.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: Visitor breaks encapsulation by exposing internal state to the visitor
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Visitor keeps operations cleanly separate from data, so encapsulation is naturally preserved."

**Why it's wrong:** for a `visitBinaryOpNode()` method to do anything useful, it needs to read `node.left`, `node.right`, and `node.op` — meaning those fields must be public, or the node class needs to expose getters specifically so external visitors can inspect its internals. This is the opposite of encapsulation: any node's internal representation is now effectively part of its public contract, because an unknown, open-ended set of future visitors need to read it.

**Correct model:** accept that Visitor trades encapsulation for extensibility — it's the right trade only when you're confident the node's structure (which fields exist) is genuinely stable, since exposing internals is the price paid to add operations without touching node classes. If the internal structure changes often too, Visitor's benefit shrinks fast.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: adding a new element type means changing every visitor
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Visitor makes the hierarchy fully extensible — I can add new node types freely, the same way I can add new operations freely."

**Why it's wrong:** adding a new node type, say `UnaryOpNode`, means the `Visitor` interface needs a new `visitUnaryOp()` method — and now every existing implementation (`PrintVisitor`, `TypeCheckVisitor`, `CodeGenVisitor`, and any others) must be updated to implement it, or the code won't compile (in a statically typed language) or will silently misbehave (in a dynamic one). This is the exact inverse of the problem Visitor solves for operations.

**Correct model:** this is Visitor's defining trade-off, not a bug — it optimizes for "operations change often, element types don't." If your actual codebase adds new element types more often than new operations, Visitor is fighting your change pattern, not helping it; use plain polymorphic methods on each class instead.
